[[File:Tietze-Moebius.svg|thumb|360px|Tietze's subdivision of a [[Möbius strip]] into six mutually-adjacent regions. The vertices and edges of the subdivision form an embedding of Tietze's graph onto the strip.]]
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[graph theory]], '''Tietze's graph''' is an [[undirected graph|undirected]] [[cubic graph|cubic]] [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] with 12 vertices and 18 edges. It is named after [[Heinrich Franz Friedrich Tietze]], who showed in 1910 that the [[Möbius strip]] can be subdivided into six regions that all touch each other – three along the boundary of the strip and three along its center line – and therefore that graphs that are [[graph embedding|embedded]] onto the Möbius strip may require six [[graph coloring|colors]].<ref>{{citation|first=Heinrich|last=Tietze|authorlink=Heinrich Franz Friedrich Tietze|url=https://sites.math.washington.edu/~mathcircle/circle/2014-15/advanced/mc-14a-w8.pdf|title=Einige Bemerkungen zum Problem des Kartenfärbens auf einseitigen Flächen|trans-title=Some remarks on the problem of map coloring on one-sided surfaces|journal=DMV Annual Report|volume=19|year=1910|pages=155–159}}</ref> The boundary segments of the regions of Tietze's subdivision (including the segments along the boundary of the Möbius strip itself) form an embedding of Tietze's graph.

==Relation to Petersen graph==
Tietze's graph may be formed from the [[Petersen graph]] by replacing one of its vertices with a triangle.<ref name="CE">{{citation|first1=L.|last1=Clark|first2=R.|last2=Entringer|title=Smallest maximally nonhamiltonian graphs|journal=Periodica Mathematica Hungarica|volume=14|issue=1|year=1983|pages=57–68|doi=10.1007/BF02023582|s2cid=122218690 }}</ref><ref>{{mathworld | urlname = TietzesGraph | title = Tietze's Graph}}</ref>
Like the Tietze graph, the Petersen graph forms the boundary of six mutually touching regions, but on the [[projective plane]] rather than on the Möbius strip. If one cuts a hole from this subdivision of the projective plane, surrounding a single vertex, the surrounded vertex is replaced by a triangle of region boundaries around the hole, giving the previously described construction of the Tietze graph.

==Hamiltonicity==
Both Tietze's graph and the Petersen graph are ''maximally nonhamiltonian'': they have no [[Hamiltonian cycle]], but any two non-adjacent vertices can be connected by a [[Hamiltonian path]].<ref name="CE"/> Tietze's graph and the Petersen graph are the only [[k-vertex-connected graph|2-vertex-connected]] cubic non-Hamiltonian graphs with 12 or fewer vertices.<ref>{{citation|first1=Narong|last1=Punnim|first2=Varaporn|last2=Saenpholphat|first3=Sermsri|last3=Thaithae|title=Almost Hamiltonian cubic graphs|journal=International Journal of Computer Science and Network Security|volume=7|issue=1|year=2007|url=http://paper.ijcsns.org/07_book/200701/200701A12.pdf|pages=83–86}}</ref>

Unlike the Petersen graph, Tietze's graph is not [[hypohamiltonian graph|hypohamiltonian]]: removing one of its three triangle vertices forms a smaller graph that remains non-Hamiltonian.

==Edge coloring and perfect matchings==
[[Edge coloring]] Tietze's graph requires four colors; that is, its chromatic index is 4. Equivalently, the edges of Tietze's graph can be partitioned into four [[matching (graph theory)|matching]]s, but no fewer.

Tietze's graph matches part of the definition of a [[snark (graph theory)|snark]]: it is a cubic [[bridgeless graph]] that is not 3-edge-colorable. However, most authors restrict snarks to graphs without 3-cycles, so Tietze's graph is not generally considered to be a snark. Nevertheless, it is [[graph isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the graph J<sub>3</sub>, part of an infinite family of [[flower snark]]s introduced by [[Rufus Isaacs (game theorist)|R. Isaacs]] in 1975.<ref>{{citation|last=Isaacs|first=R.|title=Infinite families of nontrivial trivalent graphs which are not Tait colorable|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|volume=82|pages=221–239|year=1975|doi=10.2307/2319844|jstor=2319844|issue=3|publisher=Mathematical Association of America}}.</ref>

Unlike the Petersen graph, the Tietze graph can be covered by four [[perfect matching]]s. This property plays a key role in a [[mathematical proof|proof]] that testing whether a graph can be covered by four perfect matchings is [[NP-complete]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Esperet | first1 = L.
 | last2 = Mazzuoccolo | first2 = G.
 | arxiv = 1301.6926
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Journal of Graph Theory
 | mr = 3246172
 | pages = 144–157
 | doi = 10.1002/jgt.21778
 | title = On cubic bridgeless graphs whose edge-set cannot be covered by four perfect matchings
 | volume = 77
 | year = 2014| s2cid = 15284123
 }}.</ref>

==Additional properties==
Tietze's graph has chromatic number 3, chromatic index 4, [[girth (graph theory)|girth]] 3 and [[diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] 3.  The [[independence number]] is 5. Its [[automorphism group]] has [[order (group theory)|order]] 12, and is [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the [[dihedral group]] D<sub>6</sub>, the group of symmetries of a [[regular polygon|regular]] [[hexagon]] (including both rotations and reflections).  This group has two orbits of size 3 and one of size 6 on vertices, and thus this graph is not [[vertex-transitive graph|vertex-transitive]].
